variants.name: Spring MVC DispatcherServlet
variants.implementation_notes: Spring MVC is explicitly designed around the front controller pattern: one DispatcherServlet is mapped to / (web.xml or Java config) and provides the shared algorithm, while HandlerMapping, HandlerAdapter and HandlerInterceptor beans supply dispatch, binding and cross-cutting behaviour. What replaces the classic structure: the container-managed servlet plus its delegate beans replaces the hand-written FrontController, RequestHelper and dispatcher classes, and annotated controllers (@Controller/@RestController) replace manually registered command objects.
pitfalls: Mapping DispatcherServlet to / takes over the container's default servlet, so static resources need explicit configuration; adding a second front controller in front of it duplicates dispatch.
Servlets are singletons serving concurrent requests: mutable controller or dispatcher fields are shared-state bugs.
Servlet filters run before the DispatcherServlet while HandlerInterceptors run inside it, so authentication placed in the wrong layer cannot see the mapped handler and behaves differently.

variants.name: Hand-written servlet front controller (classic J2EE)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic J2EE realization: one servlet mapped to /* implements doGet/doPost, runs the shared checks (authentication, locale, logging), resolves the request to a Command object through a helper, and forwards to the view with RequestDispatcher.forward. What replaces the classic structure: nothing - this is the raw structure from Core J2EE Patterns, still appropriate when the servlet container is the only framework available, whereas Spring's DispatcherServlet already implements the same shape for you.
pitfalls: The servlet is a singleton shared across requests: request state belongs in request or session attributes, never in instance fields.
The JSP Front Strategy (implementing the controller as a JSP page) is discouraged - control logic in markup is hard to compile, test and debug.

forward and redirect are not interchangeable: forward keeps request attributes and re-dispatches internally, redirect loses them and exposes a new URL, so mixing them per command makes navigation inconsistent.

variants.name: Spring WebFlux DispatcherHandler (reactive stack)
variants.implementation_notes: WebFlux keeps the same pattern on the reactive stack: a central WebHandler (DispatcherHandler) runs the shared algorithm, WebFilter stages wrap the exchange, HandlerMapping resolves the route and HandlerAdapter invokes it without blocking, while WebHttpHandlerBuilder assembles the processing chain. What replaces the classic structure: the dispatcher is a bean named webHandler and the route table is a RouterFunction or annotated controllers; the servlet container disappears entirely.
pitfalls: Blocking calls (JDBC, file I/O) inside the reactive chain stall the event loop - use a reactive driver or the dedicated blocking scheduler.
A filter or handler that drops the Mono instead of returning the chain silently aborts the response without an error.
Servlet-style state (ThreadLocal, request attributes) does not exist here; per-request data travels in the reactive Context or as method arguments.
